title: McNuggets, booze smuggled by drone into Canada's most secure prison: union
summary: The union representing correctional officers is raising the alarm after it says an inmate had a drone drop off a McDonald's meal and alcohol to what's supposed to be Canada's most secure prison…

image.caption: A drone delivered McDonald's chicken nuggets (not the ones pictured) fries, sauce and some alcohol to an inmate's cell window at the Sainte-Anne-des-Plaines, Que., facility this week, according to the correctional officers' union. (Shannon Stapleton/Reuters)

blocks.text: Politics·New

The union representing correctional officers is raising the alarm after it says an inmate had a drone drop off a McDonald's meal and alcohol to what's supposed to be Canada's most secure prison earlier this week.
Union says it's at 'breaking point' for illegal goods entering Quebec facility

The union said the drone delivered McDonald's chicken nuggets and fries complete with sauce and some alcohol straight to the inmate's cell window in the special handling unit at the Sainte-Anne-des-Plaines, Que., facility at around 3 a.m. on Thursday.
"The inmate found that really funny in the morning when the guards did their rounds," said Mike Bolduc, regional president of the UCCO-SACC-CSN union, in an interview.
But he's not laughing. The union has been growing increasingly concerned about contraband, from cellphones to knives, getting into the maximum security facility via drone.
"We're at the breaking point where an inmate went and delivered himself McDonald's.… What's the next thing? Is that a loaded gun? You know, it's scaring us, it's really scaring us," he said.

The inmate's unit — known as the SHU — houses extremely violent and high-risk offenders. Some of Canada's most notorious killers, like Clifford Olson and Allan Legere, spent part of their incarceration at the Quebec prison along with convicted terrorists.

items: Drug trafficker tied to minor's overdose death used drones to bring contraband into prison

blocks.text: "It's supposed to be the most secure jail in Canada and he's eating McDonald's," said Bolduc.
The details of the story were first reported on by TVA Nouvelles.
Drones are an escalating problem for Canada's penitentiary system and those who run it.
'What in the heck?' Conservative MP
Correctional Service Canada (CSC) deploys unmanned aerial vehicle detection technology at its institutions, but Bolduc said it's concerning that the radar didn't appear to detect this drone.
He thinks inmates probably get multiple drones sent out to find blind spots.
"So what happened here is that they beat the technology," said Bolduc. "The drones are incredible [with] the damage that they're causing."
The union been pushing for a far more low-tech solution: physical netting
"It's not harder than that," Bolduc said. "This now has to be a cry for help saying that we need that netting as fast as possible."
The entrance of the Sainte-Anne-des-Plaines penitentiary is shown on July 3, 2005. (Jacques Boissinot/The Canadian Press)
Bolduc said the McDonald's delivery should be a "wake-up call" for federal Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree, whose government cut $132 million from CSC's operational budget.
"I'm scared for Canadians, for their security," he said.
In a social media video Conservative MP Frank Caputo, the party's public safety critic, said the minister has been too slow on the issue of drones delivering illegal goods to prisons.
"What in the heck are we doing in Canada?" he said.
In a statement, CSC said the incident is under review but wouldn't comment on the case further, citing security considerations.
"The introduction of contraband and unauthorized items into correctional institutions remains an important issue that CSC continues to actively address," said spokesperson Kevin Antonucci.

"CSC continues to implement a multi-layered approach that includes staff vigilance, security intelligence activities, searches, detection technologies and collaboration with police and other partners."
Anandasangaree's office referred CBC News to the CSC comment.
